pos: v. (to pledge in marriage; rendering Hebrew aras)
etymology: From be- and troth, truth or pledge. To betroth is to give one's truth — a binding word given before the wedding.
biblical_def: To betroth is to pledge in marriage. In Israel betrothal was legally binding before consummation, which is why the law treats violation of a betrothed woman as adultery (Deu 22:23–24) and why Joseph, finding Mary with child, was “minded to put her away privily” (Mat 1:19). Hosea makes it the shape of covenant restoration: “I will betroth thee unto me for ever; yea, I will betroth thee unto me in righteousness, and in judgment, and in lovingkindness, and in mercies” (Hos 2:19).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines betroth as to contract to any one, in order to a future marriage; to promise or pledge one to be the future spouse of another; to affiance.
webster_full: BETROTH, v.t. To contract to any one, in order to a future marriage; to promise or pledge one to be the future spouse of another; to affiance.
2. To contract with one for a future spouse; to espouse.
3. To nominate to a bishopric, in order to consecration.
scriptures: And I will betroth thee unto me for ever; yea, I will betroth thee unto me in righteousness, and in judgment, and in lovingkindness, and in mercies.
If a damsel that is a virgin be betrothed unto an husband, and a man find her in the city, and lie with her;
Then Joseph her husband, being a just man, and not willing to make her a publick example, was minded to put her away privily.
I will even betroth thee unto me in faithfulness: and thou shalt know the LORD.
corruption_summary: Engagement is now a revocable announcement, so the biblical weight of betrothal — and with it the force of Hosea's promise — is nearly impossible to feel.
corruption_paragraphs: Hosea 2:19-20 is the more astonishing for coming where it does. God says I will betroth thee unto me for ever to a people the book has been portraying as an adulterous wife, and He lists the dowry He brings: righteousness, judgment, lovingkindness, mercies, and faithfulness. The betrothal is not a reward for reform. It is the means of it, and the last clause names the outcome: and thou shalt know the LORD.

The legal weight matters for reading Matthew 1. Joseph's dilemma was not whether to break off a casual arrangement but how to dissolve a binding covenant without destroying Mary publicly, since betrothal could only be ended by divorce or death. That he was minded to put her away privily tells us what kind of man he was before the angel ever spoke to him — a just man who preferred quiet cost to himself over public ruin for her.
roots_summary: Hebrew aras (H781), to betroth; Greek mnesteuo (G3423), to espouse — the word used of Mary and Joseph.
roots_lines: Hebrew aras (H781) — to betroth; Hosea 2:19-20, three times, Deuteronomy 20:7, 22:23.
Greek mnesteuo (G3423) — to be espoused, betrothed; Matthew 1:18, Luke 1:27, 2:5.
Greek harmozo (G718) — to join, espouse; 2 Corinthians 11:2, I have espoused you to one husband.
usage: “I will betroth thee unto me for ever” — the dowry is God's own character.
“Minded to put her away privily” — a just man's instinct before the angel spoke.
“Thou shalt know the LORD” — the betrothal's stated outcome.

pos: n. (a female slave; rendering Hebrew amah, Greek paidiske)
etymology: Bond with woman — a woman held in bondage. Paul makes the household arrangement of Genesis 16 into an allegory of two covenants.
biblical_def: A bondwoman is a female slave. Hagar is the Bible's principal one, and Sarah's demand becomes doctrine: “Cast out this bondwoman and her son: for the son of this bondwoman shall not be heir with my son” (Gen 21:10). Paul quotes it in Galatians and reads the two women as two covenants — “Abraham had two sons, the one by a bondmaid, the other by a freewoman… which things are an allegory” (Gal 4:22,24) — concluding, “we are not children of the bondwoman, but of the free” (Gal 4:31).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines bondwoman or bondmaid as a woman slave, or one born a slave.
webster_full: BONDMAID, n. A maid servant; a female slave, or one bound to service without wages.
BONDWOMAN, n. A woman slave.
scriptures: Wherefore she said unto Abraham, Cast out this bondwoman and her son: for the son of this bondwoman shall not be heir with my son, even with Isaac.
For it is written, that Abraham had two sons, the one by a bondmaid, the other by a freewoman.
Which things are an allegory: for these are the two covenants; the one from the mount Sinai, which gendereth to bondage, which is Agar.
So then, brethren, we are not children of the bondwoman, but of the free.
corruption_summary: Legalism is treated as a stricter version of the gospel, when Paul treats it as a different mother entirely — producing children who are slaves rather than heirs.
corruption_paragraphs: Galatians 4 uses the household of Abraham to make a point about how children are produced. Ishmael came by the flesh — a plan devised when the promise seemed slow — and Isaac came by promise, born to a woman past childbearing so that no one could credit the arrangement. Paul's application is that law-keeping as a means of standing produces slaves, because it can only ever generate what human effort can manage.

The conclusion is stated as an identity rather than an aspiration: so then, brethren, we are not children of the bondwoman, but of the free. That is why Paul reacts so fiercely to the Galatian drift. Adding law to grace is not a stricter discipleship; in his reading it changes which mother you were born to, and therefore whether you are an heir at all.
roots_summary: Hebrew amah (H519), a female slave or handmaid; Greek paidiske (G3814), a maidservant; eleuthera (G1658), the freewoman.
roots_lines: Hebrew amah (H519) — maidservant, bondwoman; Genesis 21:10, 12, Exodus 21:7.
Greek paidiske (G3814) — bondmaid; Galatians 4:22-31, six times.
Greek epaggelia (G1860) — promise; the means by which the free son was born.
usage: “Cast out this bondwoman and her son” — Sarah's demand, quoted as scripture.
“Which things are an allegory” — two women, two covenants.
“We are not children of the bondwoman, but of the free” — stated as identity.

pos: n. (a woman not in bondage; rendering Greek eleuthera)
etymology: Free with woman. The term exists in the KJV almost solely for Paul's Galatians allegory, where legal status carries covenant meaning.
biblical_def: A freewoman is one not held in bondage. Paul sets her against the bondwoman: “Abraham had two sons, the one by a bondmaid, the other by a freewoman. But he who was of the bondwoman was born after the flesh; but he of the freewoman was by promise” (Gal 4:22–23). Sarah stands for “Jerusalem which is above… which is the mother of us all” (Gal 4:26), and the chapter ends by assigning believers their parentage: “we are not children of the bondwoman, but of the free” (Gal 4:31).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines freewoman as a woman not a slave; and free as being at liberty, not being under necessity or restraint.
webster_full: FREEWOMAN, n. A woman not a slave.
FREE, a. Being at liberty; not being under necessity or restraint, physical or moral.
2. In government, not enslaved; not in a state of vassalage or dependence.
scriptures: For it is written, that Abraham had two sons, the one by a bondmaid, the other by a freewoman.
But he who was of the bondwoman was born after the flesh; but he of the freewoman was by promise.
But Jerusalem which is above is free, which is the mother of us all.
So then, brethren, we are not children of the bondwoman, but of the free.
corruption_summary: Christian liberty is preached as permission rather than parentage, when Paul roots it in who bore you — a status that cannot be earned and therefore cannot be forfeited by failure.
corruption_paragraphs: Galatians 4:26 makes the freewoman a city: Jerusalem which is above is free, which is the mother of us all. Paul is not offering believers a looser rulebook; he is telling them where they were born. Liberty in this argument is a birth certificate, not a licence, which is why he can turn immediately in chapter 5 to warn against using liberty for an occasion to the flesh without contradicting himself.

The promise-versus-flesh contrast in verse 23 is the engine of the whole passage. He who was of the bondwoman was born after the flesh; but he of the freewoman was by promise. Isaac's birth required a miracle because Sarah was past age; Ishmael's required only a human arrangement. Anything the flesh can produce, the flesh will eventually claim credit for — which is precisely why God arranged a birth that no one could.
roots_summary: Greek eleuthera (G1658), free, a freewoman; eleutheria (G1657), liberty — the theme word of Galatians 5:1.
roots_lines: Greek eleuthera (G1658) — free, freewoman; Galatians 4:22-31.
Greek eleutheria (G1657) — liberty; Galatians 5:1, stand fast therefore in the liberty wherewith Christ hath made us free.
Greek ano (G507) — above; Jerusalem which is above, Galatians 4:26.
usage: “The other by a freewoman” — two sons, two principles.
“Jerusalem which is above is free, which is the mother of us all” — liberty as parentage.
“He of the freewoman was by promise” — a birth the flesh could not claim.

pos: n. (a female blood relative; rendering Hebrew shearah)
etymology: Kin with woman. The term appears chiefly in the law's boundaries around family relations.
biblical_def: A kinswoman is a female relative. Leviticus uses the word to fence marriage and sexual relations within a household: “Thou shalt not uncover the nakedness of thy father's sister: she is thy father's near kinswoman” (Lev 18:12–13). Proverbs turns kinship into an image of intimacy with wisdom: “Say unto wisdom, Thou art my sister; and call understanding thy kinswoman” (Pro 7:4) — and the reason follows: to keep thee from the strange woman.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines kinswoman as a female relation.
webster_full: KINSWOMAN, n. A female relation.
KIN, n. Relation, properly by consanguinity or blood; kindred.
scriptures: Thou shalt not uncover the nakedness of thy father's sister: she is thy father's near kinswoman.
Thou shalt not uncover the nakedness of thy mother's sister: for she is thy mother's near kinswoman.
Say unto wisdom, Thou art my sister; and call understanding thy kinswoman:
That they may keep thee from the strange woman, from the stranger which flattereth with her words.
corruption_summary: Household boundaries are treated as arbitrary taboo, when Leviticus 18 protects the very people least able to refuse — the young and dependent inside a family.
corruption_paragraphs: Leviticus 18's list of forbidden relations is often skimmed as primitive taboo, but its logic is protective. The relationships named are precisely those in which one party has power and proximity over another who cannot easily refuse or escape: a father's household, an uncle's authority, a brother's house. Fencing the family is how the vulnerable within it are kept safe, and a culture that dissolves those fences in the name of freedom is exposing exactly the people the law shielded.

Proverbs 7:4 makes the surprising move of putting wisdom inside the family circle. Say unto wisdom, Thou art my sister; and call understanding thy kinswoman: that they may keep thee from the strange woman. The strategy is not to think harder about temptation in the moment but to have an established intimacy with wisdom beforehand — the kind of familiarity a man has with a sister, which makes the seduction of a stranger less compelling.
roots_summary: Hebrew shearah (H7608), a near kinswoman, from sheer, flesh or blood relation; modaath (H4129), kindred, in Ruth 3:2.
roots_lines: Hebrew shearah (H7608) — near kinswoman; Leviticus 18:17, 20:19.
Hebrew sheer (H7607) — flesh, blood relation; Leviticus 18:12-13, she is thy father's near kinswoman.
Hebrew modaath (H4129) — kindred, acquaintance; Ruth 3:2, is not Boaz of our kindred?
usage: “She is thy father's near kinswoman” — the household fenced.
“Call understanding thy kinswoman” — wisdom brought inside the family.
“That they may keep thee from the strange woman” — the stated purpose.

etymology: Brother with the adjectival ending. The Greek compound — love of brother — gave a Pennsylvania city its name and the New Testament a command.
biblical_def: Brotherly describes affection between believers. Paul commands it with a competitive twist: “Be kindly affectioned one to another with brotherly love; in honour preferring one another” (Rom 12:10). Hebrews opens its closing exhortations with “Let brotherly love continue” (Heb 13:1). Peter places it as the second-to-last rung of Christian growth, adding charity above it (2Pe 1:7), and notes the Thessalonians needed no instruction in it because “ye yourselves are taught of God to love one another” (1Th 4:9).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines brotherly as pertaining to brothers; such as is natural for brothers; becoming brothers; kind; affectionate.
webster_full: BROTHERLY, a. Pertaining to brothers; such as is natural for brothers; becoming brothers; kind; affectionate; as brotherly love.
scriptures: Be kindly affectioned one to another with brotherly love; in honour preferring one another;
And to godliness brotherly kindness; and to brotherly kindness charity.
But as touching brotherly love ye need not that I write unto you: for ye yourselves are taught of God to love one another.
corruption_summary: Congregational warmth is engineered through programming, when the New Testament assumes brotherly love as a family fact and commands only that it continue.
corruption_paragraphs: Hebrews 13:1 is remarkably brief: let brotherly love continue. Not begin, not increase — continue. The assumption is that it already exists, being the natural affection of people who share a Father, and the danger addressed is erosion rather than absence. The verses that follow show what continuing looks like in practice: hospitality to strangers, remembering prisoners as bound with them, and honouring marriage. Affection is measured in inconvenience.

Romans 12:10 adds the competitive clause that makes it costly: in honour preferring one another. The instinct is to seek honour; the command is to hand it over, and to compete at handing it over. A congregation where members actively work to put one another forward looks nothing like an organization, and it cannot be produced by any program — only by people who genuinely believe they are related.
roots_summary: Greek philadelphia (G5360), brotherly love; philostorgos (G5387), tenderly affectioned as family — Romans 12:10 uses both.
roots_lines: Greek philadelphia (G5360) — brotherly love; Romans 12:10, Hebrews 13:1, 1 Thessalonians 4:9, 2 Peter 1:7.
Greek philostorgos (G5387) — tenderly loving, of family affection; only Romans 12:10.
Greek agape (G26) — charity, love; the rung Peter places above brotherly kindness.
usage: “Let brotherly love continue” — assumed present, guarded against erosion.
“In honour preferring one another” — competing to hand honour away.
“Ye yourselves are taught of God to love one another” — the instruction was not Paul's.

etymology: Child with the privative ending. In a culture where lineage carried covenant promise, childlessness was grief and apparent exclusion at once.
biblical_def: Childless means without offspring. Abram states it as his objection to God's promise: “Lord GOD, what wilt thou give me, seeing I go childless?” (Gen 15:2). It appears as a judicial sentence — Jeremiah writes of Coniah, “Write ye this man childless” (Jer 22:30) — and in the law as a penalty (Lev 20:20–21). Isaiah answers the grief directly: “unto them will I give in mine house and within my walls a place and a name better than of sons and of daughters” (Isa 56:5).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines childless as destitute of children or offspring.
webster_full: CHILDLESS, a. Destitute of children or offspring.
scriptures: And Abram said, Lord GOD, what wilt thou give me, seeing I go childless, and the steward of my house is this Eliezer of Damascus?
Even unto them will I give in mine house and within my walls a place and a name better than of sons and of daughters: I will give them an everlasting name, that shall not be cut off.
Thus saith the LORD, Write ye this man childless, a man that shall not prosper in his days: for no man of his seed shall prosper, sitting upon the throne of David, and ruling any more in Judah.

Sing, O barren, thou that didst not bear; break forth into singing, and cry aloud, thou that didst not travail with child: for more are the children of the desolate than the children of the married wife, saith the LORD.
corruption_summary: Churches built entirely around families can make the childless feel like spectators, while Isaiah 56 promises them a name in God's house better than sons and daughters.
corruption_paragraphs: Isaiah 56:3-5 addresses two groups who had reason to believe they were structurally excluded — the foreigner and the eunuch — and the promise to the second is startlingly specific: neither let the eunuch say, Behold, I am a dry tree. For thus saith the LORD unto the eunuchs that keep my sabbaths… even unto them will I give in mine house and within my walls a place and a name better than of sons and of daughters: I will give them an everlasting name, that shall not be cut off. The word for name is the same root as memorial. God offers permanence to those who cannot pass on a name.

Genesis 15:2 shows the honesty Scripture permits in the meantime. Abram does not pretend the promise satisfies him while his house remains empty; he says what wilt thou give me, seeing I go childless, and God takes him outside to look at the stars. Grief stated plainly to God is not unbelief, and Isaiah 54's command to the barren woman — sing, O barren, thou that didst not bear — is given before anything has visibly changed.
roots_summary: Hebrew ariri (H6185), stripped, childless; shakol (H7921), to be bereaved of children.
roots_lines: Hebrew ariri (H6185) — childless; Genesis 15:2, Leviticus 20:20-21, Jeremiah 22:30.
Hebrew aqarah (H6135) — barren; Isaiah 54:1, sing, O barren, thou that didst not bear.
Hebrew yad vashem — a place and a name; Isaiah 56:5, better than of sons and of daughters.
usage: “What wilt thou give me, seeing I go childless?” — grief stated plainly to God.
“A place and a name better than of sons and of daughters” — permanence promised.
“Write ye this man childless” — the sentence on Coniah.

pos: n. (interment of the dead; rendering Hebrew qeburah, Greek entaphiasmos)
etymology: From Old English byrgan, to bury. Burial in Scripture is an act of honour, and its denial is treated as a curse.
biblical_def: Burial is the interment of the dead, and Scripture treats it as a duty of honour. Abraham buys a field to bury Sarah rather than accept it as a gift (Gen 23:16–19). Denial of burial is a judgment: Jehoiakim shall have “the burial of an ass, drawn and cast forth beyond the gates of Jerusalem” (Jer 22:19). Christ interprets the anointing at Bethany as advance work: “she did it for my burial” (Mat 26:12), and Joseph of Arimathea supplies a new tomb (Mat 27:59–60).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines burial as the act of burying a deceased person; sepulture; interment; the act of depositing a dead body in the earth, in a tomb or vault.
webster_full: BURIAL, n. The act of burying a deceased person; sepulture; interment; the act of depositing a dead body in the earth, in a tomb or vault, or in the water.
2. The act of placing any thing under earth or water.
scriptures: And after this, Abraham buried Sarah his wife in the cave of the field of Machpelah before Mamre: the same is Hebron in the land of Canaan.
He shall be buried with the burial of an ass, drawn and cast forth beyond the gates of Jerusalem.
For in that she hath poured this ointment on my body, she did it for my burial.
And that he was buried, and that he rose again the third day according to the scriptures:
corruption_summary: Death is outsourced and hurried past, where Scripture slows down for it — giving whole chapters to the purchase of a grave and the wrapping of a body.
corruption_paragraphs: Genesis 23 spends an entire chapter on a real-estate transaction for a burial plot, which seems disproportionate until the theology is noticed. Abraham, promised the whole land, owns none of it, and the first parcel he legally acquires is a grave. He insists on paying full price — four hundred shekels of silver, current money with the merchant — so that his claim cannot be questioned. Faith buys a tomb in a country it has been promised but does not yet possess.

1 Corinthians 15:4 makes burial part of the gospel's minimum content: that he was buried, and that he rose again the third day according to the scriptures. The burial is not an incidental detail between the two events; it is the evidence that the death was real and complete, attested by the men who wrapped the body and the women who watched where He was laid. Christianity's central claim requires a grave that was genuinely occupied before it was found empty.
roots_summary: Hebrew qeburah (H6900), a grave or burial; Greek entaphiasmos (G1780), preparation for burial — the word Christ applies to the ointment at Bethany.
roots_lines: Hebrew qeburah (H6900) — burial, grave; Genesis 35:20, Jeremiah 22:19, the burial of an ass.
Greek entaphiasmos (G1780) — preparing for burial; Mark 14:8, John 12:7.
Greek thapto (G2290) — to bury; 1 Corinthians 15:4, and that he was buried.
usage: “The field, and the cave that is therein, were made sure unto Abraham” — faith buys a grave.
“She did it for my burial” — the ointment read as preparation.
“That he was buried, and that he rose again” — the grave inside the gospel.

etymology: A variant of band, from bind. A bond may be a shackle or a ligament — Scripture uses both senses, and the difference is everything.
biblical_def: A bond is that which binds. Paul makes it the church's connective tissue: believers are to endeavour “to keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace” (Eph 4:3), and above all the virtues to “put on charity, which is the bond of perfectness” (Col 3:14). He also writes as a prisoner, asking prayer and mentioning “my bonds in Christ” (Php 1:13). Isaiah's chosen fast is “to loose the bands of wickedness, to undo the heavy burdens” (Isa 58:6).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines bond as any thing that binds, as a cord, chain, rope or band; and figuratively, a cause of union, cement of union.
webster_full: BOND, n. Any thing that binds, as a cord, a chain, a rope; a band.
2. Ligament; that which holds things together.
3. Union; connection; a binding.
4. Cause of union; cement which unites; link of connection.
scriptures: Endeavouring to keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace.
And above all these things put on charity, which is the bond of perfectness.
So that my bonds in Christ are manifest in all the palace, and in all other places;
Is not this the fast that I have chosen? to loose the bands of wickedness, to undo the heavy burdens, and to let the oppressed go free, and that ye break every yoke?
corruption_summary: Unity is pursued by agreement on everything or by ignoring difference, when Paul locates it in a bond — something that holds pieces together precisely because they are distinct.
corruption_paragraphs: Ephesians 4:3 uses a verb of effort: endeavouring to keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace. The unity is not created by the church; it is the Spirit's, already given, and the congregation's work is to keep it. The bond that does the holding is peace, which means the practical labour of unity is the labour of peacemaking — forbearing, forgiving, lowliness and meekness, all listed in the verse before.

Colossians 3:14 goes further: above all these things put on charity, which is the bond of perfectness. Paul has just listed mercies, kindness, humbleness, meekness, longsuffering, forbearing, forgiving — and then names love as the belt that holds the whole outfit on. Without it the virtues fall off one at a time. That is why the New Testament never treats love as one virtue among several; it is the fastening for all of them.
roots_summary: Greek sundesmos (G4886), that which binds together, a ligament; desmos (G1199), a chain or imprisonment — the same root, opposite experience.
roots_lines: Greek sundesmos (G4886) — bond, ligament; Ephesians 4:3, Colossians 2:19, 3:14.
Greek desmos (G1199) — bond, chain; Philippians 1:13, my bonds in Christ are manifest in all the palace.
Hebrew mosarah (H4147) — band, bond; Isaiah 58:6, to loose the bands of wickedness.
usage: “The unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace” — unity kept, not manufactured.
“Charity, which is the bond of perfectness” — the belt that holds the outfit on.
“To loose the bands of wickedness” — the fast God chooses.

pos: n. (one personally known; rendering Hebrew yada, to know)
etymology: From Old French acointance, familiarity. In Scripture acquaintance sits between stranger and friend, and the psalms make much of its failure.
biblical_def: An acquaintance is one personally known. Job's are among his losses: “He hath put my brethren far from me, and mine acquaintance are verily estranged from me” (Job 19:13). David's sharpest grief is of a familiar friend: “it was not an enemy that reproached me… but it was thou, a man mine equal, my guide, and mine acquaintance” (Psa 55:12–13). Eliphaz offers the good advice he does not himself follow: “Acquaint now thyself with him, and be at peace” (Job 22:21). Luke notes that Christ's acquaintance stood afar off at the cross (Luk 23:49).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines acquaintance as familiar knowledge; a state of being acquainted; and a person or persons well known.
webster_full: ACQUAINTANCE, n. Familiar knowledge; a state of being acquainted, or of having intimate or more than slight or superficial knowledge.
2. A person or persons well known; usually persons we have been accustomed to see and converse with.
scriptures: But it was thou, a man mine equal, my guide, and mine acquaintance.
He hath put my brethren far from me, and mine acquaintance are verily estranged from me.
Acquaint now thyself with him, and be at peace: thereby good shall come unto thee. him: that is, God
And all his acquaintance, and the women that followed him from Galilee, stood afar off, beholding these things.
corruption_summary: Wide acquaintance is mistaken for friendship, and a person may be known by hundreds while Psalm 55's betrayal — by one who actually knew him — remains the deeper wound.
corruption_paragraphs: Psalm 55:12-14 explains why betrayal by an acquaintance cuts differently than opposition from an enemy. For it was not an enemy that reproached me; then I could have borne it… but it was thou, a man mine equal, my guide, and mine acquaintance. We took sweet counsel together, and walked unto the house of God in company. The pain is proportional to the access granted. An enemy's blow lands on armour; an acquaintance's lands where the armour was taken off.

Job 22:21 puts the word to its best use, even though Eliphaz was a poor counsellor: acquaint now thyself with him, and be at peace: thereby good shall come unto thee. Acquaintance with God is offered as something a man may deliberately pursue rather than passively receive. The verb assumes a Person who can be known by degrees, which is the difference between religion and a relationship.
roots_summary: Hebrew yada (H3045), to know; meyudda (H3045), an acquaintance, one known; Greek gnostos (G1110), known, an acquaintance.
roots_lines: Hebrew yada (H3045) — to know; Job 22:21, acquaint now thyself with him.
Hebrew meyudda — acquaintance, familiar friend; Psalm 55:13, Job 19:14, 2 Kings 12:5.
Greek gnostos (G1110) — known, acquaintance; Luke 2:44, 23:49.
usage: “A man mine equal, my guide, and mine acquaintance” — the blow lands where armour was off.
“Acquaint now thyself with him, and be at peace” — a Person known by degrees.
“All his acquaintance… stood afar off” — at the cross.
